meta.author: bank-team-integrated-3
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify when a sample claim exceeds its evidence
questions.stem: A warehouse manager samples 40 pallets from one dock and claims all docks meet spec; which flaw is present?

options.text: Sampling one dock cannot support a claim about every dock in the plant
The sample is too small to estimate the mean weight of a single pallet
The manager should have used a census of all pallets on that dock
options.misconception: treats one dock as the whole population

options.text: The claim is valid because 40 pallets exceed the usual minimum sample size

questions.explanation: Sampling from one dock only supports claims about that dock. Extending the conclusion to all docks overreaches the evidence collected.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sample mirrors the full population.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise untestable assumptions in a model
questions.stem: A report assumes customer demand is independent of price; what is the main risk?

options.text: The assumption is trivial and can be verified from past invoices
Independence only matters for categorical variables, not demand
Demand likely depends on price so the model may mislead decisions
The assumption is harmless because all models need simplifying shortcuts

questions.explanation: Price and demand often interact, so an untestable independence assumption can distort forecasts and downstream choices.
questions.hint: Check whether the assumption could be contradicted by data.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a path probability from a tree
questions.stem: A tree shows stage one success probability 0.6 and stage two success 0.5; what is the joint success probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply along the path: 0.6 times 0.5 equals 0.30. This is the chance both stages succeed.
questions.hint: Multiply branch probabilities along the path.

questions.stem: Of 200 orders, 80 are late and 50 of those are international; what is P(international | late)?
questions.explanation: Divide the joint count by the condition count: 50 divided by 80 equals 0.625. This is the share of late orders that are international.
questions.hint: Divide joint count by the condition count.

questions.learningObjective: State the mean of a binomial distribution
questions.stem: Explain why the expected number of successes in n trials with success probability p is n times p.

answer.exemplar: Each trial contributes an expected 1 times p plus 0 times (1-p), which equals p; with n independent trials linearity of expectation gives n times p successes on average.

questions.explanation: Linearity of expectation lets us add each trial's expected contribution. Every trial expects p successes, so n trials expect n times p.
questions.hint: Add the expected contribution of each trial.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the empirical rule to a normal mean
questions.stem: A process mean is 100 with standard deviation 5; about what percent of values lie within one standard deviation?

options.text: About 50 percent of values fall between 95 and 105
options.misconception: confuses centre mass with median split

options.text: About 95 percent of values fall between 95 and 105
options.misconception: uses the two-sigma figure for one sigma

options.text: About 99.7 percent of values fall between 95 and 105
options.misconception: uses the three-sigma figure for one sigma

options.text: About 68 percent of values fall between 95 and 105

questions.explanation: The empirical rule places about 68 percent within one standard deviation. The other options apply wrong sigma multipliers.
questions.hint: Recall the 68-95-99.7 rule.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Estimate a tail probability using the rule
questions.stem: For a normal score two standard deviations above the mean, roughly what percent of values exceed it?

options.text: About 16 percent of values exceed two standard deviations above
options.misconception: uses one-sigma tail for two sigma

options.text: About 5 percent of values exceed two standard deviations above
About 2.5 percent of values exceed two standard deviations above
About 0.15 percent of values exceed two standard deviations above
options.misconception: uses three-sigma tail for two sigma

questions.explanation: About 95 percent lie within two sigma, leaving 5 percent in both tails, so roughly 2.5 percent exceed the upper bound.
questions.hint: Split the remaining tail mass evenly.

questions.stem: A colleague divides the sample standard deviation by n instead of root n; what goes wrong?

options.text: Standard deviation should never be divided at all
Nothing changes because n and root n are nearly equal for large samples
The value becomes larger, making intervals overly conservative
options.misconception: reverses the effect of the error

options.text: The reported spread is too small and intervals become too narrow

questions.explanation: Dividing by n shrinks the spread far more than dividing by root n. Intervals then undercover the true mean.
questions.hint: Compare n with its square root.

questions.stem: A survey of 500 adults claims teenagers prefer a new app, but only 30 respondents were teenagers; critique the claim.

answer.exemplar: The subgroup of 30 teenagers is too small for a stable estimate, and the sampling method may not represent teenagers, so the claim is unsupported.

questions.explanation: A small subgroup gives a noisy estimate and the sample may not mirror the target group. The claim therefore exceeds the evidence.
questions.hint: Check the subgroup size and representativeness.

questions.stem: If a model assumes zero correlation between two drivers with actual correlation 0.4, by how much is the combined variance understated in standard deviation units if each variance is 1?
questions.explanation: Combined variance with zero correlation is 2; with correlation 0.4 it is 2.4. The understatement in variance is 0.4, one standard deviation unit effect.
questions.hint: Compare variance with and without the correlation term.

questions.learningObjective: Sum path probabilities for an event
questions.stem: A tree has two paths to success with probabilities 0.12 and 0.18; what is the total success probability?
questions.explanation: Add the mutually exclusive path probabilities: 0.12 plus 0.18 equals 0.30. This is the total chance of success.
questions.hint: Add probabilities of disjoint paths.

questions.stem: Given P(A)=0.3, P(B|A)=0.5 and P(B)=0.4, what is P(A|B)?
questions.explanation: Bayes gives 0.3 times 0.5 divided by 0.4, which is 0.375. The other options misuse the given probabilities.
questions.hint: Apply Bayes theorem with the given values.

questions.stem: For 5 trials with success probability 0.2, what is the probability of exactly 2 successes?
questions.explanation: C(5,2) times 0.2 squared times 0.8 cubed equals 10 times 0.04 times 0.512, which is 0.2048. The formula accounts for all orderings.
questions.hint: Include the combination and both success and failure terms.

questions.learningObjective: Use the rule for an interval
questions.stem: A report states about 95 percent of measurements fall within two standard deviations; is this right for a normal process?

options.text: No, the correct figure is 99.7 percent for two standard deviations
No, the correct figure is 68 percent for two standard deviations
options.misconception: swaps one and two sigma figures

options.text: Yes, roughly 95 percent lie within two standard deviations of the mean
No, the rule only applies to sample means, not measurements

questions.explanation: The empirical rule gives about 95 percent within two standard deviations. The other options misstate the percentage or scope.
questions.hint: Recall the 68-95-99.7 percentages.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Describe how the empirical rule helps judge whether a data set is roughly normal.

answer.exemplar: Compare the observed shares within one, two, and three standard deviations with 68, 95, and 99.7 percent; close agreement suggests approximate normality.

questions.explanation: The rule gives benchmark shares for a normal distribution. Observed shares close to those benchmarks support approximate normality.
questions.hint: Match observed shares to the benchmark percentages.

questions.stem: A sample of 64 has standard deviation 8; what is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of n: 8 divided by 8 equals 1. This is the standard error.
questions.hint: Divide standard deviation by square root of n.

questions.stem: A pilot group of 12 volunteers shows improved scores; can we claim all employees improve?

options.text: No, only randomised experiments can show improvement
options.misconception: overstates the requirement for any claim

options.text: Yes, any improvement in a pilot proves the programme works everywhere
options.misconception: generalises from a small volunteer sample

options.text: Yes, because 12 exceeds the minimum for a t-test
No, volunteers may differ from all employees and the group is small

questions.explanation: Volunteers and small groups may not represent all employees. The claim overreaches the available evidence.
questions.hint: Consider selection bias and sample size.

questions.stem: A forecast assumes no competitor enters the market; which statement best describes this assumption?

options.text: It is testable today by surveying competitor intentions
It is untestable now but could be checked once the horizon passes
It is not an assumption because it is written in the report
It is harmless because forecasts are always uncertain anyway

questions.explanation: The assumption cannot be verified until the period ends, though it may be checked later. It still carries risk now.
questions.hint: Decide whether evidence exists today.

questions.stem: A tree gives P(rain)=0.3 and P(delay|rain)=0.4; what is P(rain and delay)?
questions.explanation: Multiply the marginal and conditional probabilities: 0.3 times 0.4 equals 0.12. This is the joint chance.
questions.hint: Multiply the stage probabilities.

questions.stem: Of 120 tickets, 30 are urgent and 12 urgent ones are escalated; what is P(escalated | urgent)?
questions.explanation: Divide the escalated urgent count by all urgent tickets: 12 divided by 30 equals 0.40. That is the conditional share.
questions.hint: Divide the joint count by the condition count.

questions.stem: A report models daily sales counts as binomial but probabilities change by season; what is the issue?

options.text: Seasonality only affects the mean, not the distribution shape
options.misconception: understates the effect of changing p

options.text: Binomial counts cannot exceed the number of trials
options.misconception: states a true but irrelevant bound

options.text: The binomial model needs a constant success probability across trials
Sales are continuous, so Poisson is always better

questions.explanation: A binomial requires a fixed success probability. Seasonal changes in p violate that condition and bias the model.
questions.hint: Check whether p stays constant.

questions.learningObjective: Estimate a range from the rule
questions.stem: A normal measurement has mean 50 and standard deviation 4; about what range covers 95 percent?
questions.explanation: Two standard deviations each way gives 50 minus 8 to 50 plus 8, or 42 to 58. That covers about 95 percent.
questions.hint: Use mean plus or minus two standard deviations.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Why does the normal distribution have thin tails compared with many real data sets?

answer.exemplar: The normal density decays exponentially in squared distance, so extreme values become very unlikely, while real processes often produce heavier tails.

questions.explanation: Normal tails shrink rapidly because probability falls with squared distance. Real data often contain more extreme outcomes.
questions.hint: Consider how probability changes with distance from the mean.

questions.stem: What happens to the sampling distribution of the mean as sample size grows?

options.text: It becomes more skewed and its spread grows
It becomes more normal and its spread shrinks
It stays identical to the population distribution
It converges to the population standard deviation
options.misconception: confuses mean distribution with spread value

questions.explanation: The central limit theorem makes the mean distribution more normal, and larger n reduces its standard error.
questions.hint: Recall the central limit theorem.

questions.stem: An observational sample shows higher sales after a price cut; can the report claim the cut caused it?

options.text: Yes, because the sample size is large enough
Yes, the timing proves the price cut drove sales
No, other factors could explain the increase without a controlled comparison
No, observational data can never describe sales

questions.explanation: Without controlling for confounders, the observed association may not be causal. The claim overreaches the design.
questions.hint: Ask whether confounders were controlled.

questions.stem: If a model assumes a growth rate of 5 percent and actual growth is 3 percent, by how many percentage points is the forecast overstated after one year on a 100 base?
questions.explanation: The forecast predicts 105 while reality reaches 103, a two-point overstatement on the 100 base. The assumption error drives the gap.
questions.hint: Subtract actual from assumed growth on the base.

questions.stem: A machine has two failure modes with probabilities 0.05 and 0.03, and both cannot occur together; what is total failure probability?
questions.explanation: Add the disjoint probabilities: 0.05 plus 0.03 equals 0.08. This is the total failure chance.
questions.hint: Add probabilities of disjoint events.

questions.stem: A report says P(fraud | flagged)=0.9 and concludes 90 percent of all transactions are fraud; what is wrong?

options.text: The conclusion is correct because 0.9 is high
The probability should have been squared to cover both directions
Flagging is random, so the conditional is meaningless
The 90 percent applies only to flagged transactions, not all transactions

questions.explanation: The conditional probability restricts to flagged transactions. Extending it to all transactions confuses the condition with the population.
questions.hint: Notice what event the probability is conditioned on.

questions.stem: For 10 trials with success probability 0.4, what is the variance of the success count?
questions.explanation: Variance equals n times p times (1-p): 10 times 0.4 times 0.6 equals 2.4. This measures spread of the count.
questions.hint: Use n p (1-p).

questions.learningObjective: Identify an outlier using the rule
questions.stem: A value lies four standard deviations above the mean; how should a normal report treat it?

options.text: It is expected in about 5 percent of normal observations
It is extremely unusual and warrants checking for error or special cause
It is impossible under a normal model
It should be deleted automatically to protect the mean

questions.explanation: Four sigma is far beyond the usual range, so it is extremely unusual. It deserves investigation rather than automatic deletion.
questions.hint: Consider how rare four sigma is.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: A value of 112 comes from a normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 6; what is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation: (112-100)/6 equals 2. The z-score is 2.
questions.hint: Subtract mean then divide by standard deviation.

questions.stem: Why do different samples from the same population yield different means?

answer.exemplar: Random selection includes different individuals each time, so the average varies from sample to sample around the population mean.

questions.explanation: Each sample contains a different subset of individuals. Their average therefore varies around the true population mean.
questions.hint: Think about who gets included in each sample.

questions.stem: A study of 200 hospital patients claims all adults in the country have the condition; what is the flaw?

options.text: Hospitals always overcount conditions, so the data are useless
The sample size is too small for any statistical conclusion
Hospital patients are not representative of all adults in the country
The claim is fine because 200 exceeds common minimums

questions.explanation: Hospital patients differ systematically from the general adult population. The claim overreaches the sample's coverage.
questions.hint: Consider who is included in the sample.

questions.stem: A model assumes future regulation will not change; how should a report treat this?

options.text: Remove it from the model to avoid the issue
options.misconception: solves by omission rather than analysis

options.text: Ignore it because all forecasts contain uncertainty
Treat it as a fact since no change is planned today
options.misconception: confuses current plans with future outcomes

options.text: Flag it as an untestable assumption with a sensitivity check

questions.explanation: The assumption cannot be verified now, so the report should flag it and test sensitivity. Ignoring or removing it hides risk.
questions.hint: Decide how to handle an unverifiable premise.

questions.stem: In a probability tree, what do the numbers on branches represent?

options.text: Counts of observations at each stage
Conditional or marginal probabilities for each stage
Cumulative probabilities from the root
Odds ratios between adjacent stages

questions.explanation: Branch labels are probabilities for that stage, sometimes conditional. They are not counts, totals, or odds ratios.
questions.hint: Recall what a branch probability means.

questions.stem: If P(A)=0.5 and P(B|A)=0.6, what is P(A and B)?
questions.explanation: Multiply the marginal and conditional probabilities: 0.5 times 0.6 equals 0.30. This is the joint probability.
questions.hint: Multiply P(A) by P(B given A).

questions.stem: For 20 trials with success probability 0.35, what is the expected number of successes?
questions.explanation: Multiply n by p: 20 times 0.35 equals 7. This is the expected success count.
questions.hint: Multiply trials by success probability.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the rule to a tail
questions.stem: About what percent of normal values exceed one standard deviation above the mean?

options.text: About 2.5 percent
options.misconception: uses two-sigma tail for one sigma

options.text: About 32 percent
options.misconception: uses the full one-sigma band as a tail

options.text: About 16 percent
About 50 percent

questions.explanation: About 68 percent lie within one sigma, leaving 32 percent in both tails, so roughly 16 percent exceed the upper bound.
questions.hint: Split the outside share evenly.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: A normal score has mean 80 and standard deviation 10; about what percent fall between 60 and 100?

options.text: About 50 percent
About 68 percent
About 99.7 percent
About 95 percent

questions.explanation: 60 to 100 is mean plus or minus two standard deviations, covering about 95 percent. The other options use wrong widths.
questions.hint: Count standard deviations from the mean.

questions.learningObjective: Compute probability for a sample mean
questions.stem: With standard error 2, what z-score corresponds to a sample mean 4 above the population mean?
questions.explanation: Divide the difference by the standard error: 4 divided by 2 equals 2. The z-score for the sample mean is 2.
questions.hint: Divide the difference by the standard error.

questions.stem: A report studies only surviving companies to claim the industry is healthy; what bias is present?

answer.exemplar: Survivorship bias: failed firms are excluded, so the sample overstates health and cannot support a claim about the whole industry.

questions.explanation: Excluding failed firms skews the sample toward survivors. The claim about the whole industry is unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask which cases are missing from the sample.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an assumption in a statistical model?

options.text: A result proven by the data and reported as significant
A condition accepted without direct evidence that affects conclusions
A variable that was measured but not used in the model
A calculation error that can be fixed by re-running code

questions.explanation: An assumption is accepted without direct evidence and shapes conclusions. It is not a finding, unused variable, or bug.
questions.hint: Focus on what is taken for granted.

questions.stem: A tree path to failure has probability 0.2; what is the probability of the complementary success path if these are the only two outcomes?
questions.explanation: The complement of 0.2 is 1 minus 0.2, which equals 0.8. That is the success probability.
questions.hint: Subtract from one.

questions.stem: Of 150 clients, 60 are new and 24 of those are premium; what is P(premium | new)?

options.misconception: divides new count by premium count

questions.explanation: Divide premium new clients by all new clients: 24 divided by 60 equals 0.40. This is the conditional probability.
questions.hint: Divide joint count by the condition count.

questions.stem: A colleague says the expected successes in 50 trials with p=0.2 is 50 plus 0.2; what is wrong?

options.text: No formula is needed; just simulate
The formula should use (1-p) instead of p
Expectation equals the variance for a binomial
Expectation is the product, not the sum, of n and p

questions.explanation: The expected count is n times p, not n plus p. Adding misstates the linear expectation.
questions.hint: Multiply trials by success probability.

questions.stem: State the empirical rule for a normal distribution in terms of standard deviations.

answer.exemplar: About 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation, 95 percent within two, and 99.7 percent within three standard deviations of the mean.

questions.explanation: The rule gives benchmark shares for one, two, and three standard deviations. These are the standard reference points.
questions.hint: Recall 68, 95, and 99.7 percent.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: A data set shows 85 percent within one standard deviation; how does that compare with a normal model?

options.text: It matches the normal model exactly
It is more concentrated near the centre than a normal model predicts
It is more spread out than a normal model predicts
The comparison is impossible without the median

questions.explanation: A normal model expects about 68 percent within one sigma. Observing 85 percent indicates more central concentration.
questions.hint: Compare the observed share with 68 percent.

questions.stem: A sample of 100 has standard deviation 15; what is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of n: 15 divided by 10 equals 1.5. This is the standard error.
questions.hint: Divide standard deviation by square root of n.

questions.stem: A model fitted to 2020-2024 sales is used to predict 2035 sales; what is the main concern?

options.text: Predictions are always accurate for linear models
The model is invalid because it uses only five years of data
options.misconception: blames sample size rather than range

options.text: Extrapolating far beyond the observed range risks large error
The concern is only about rounding in the output

questions.explanation: Predicting far outside the observed range extrapolates into unknown conditions. The claim is not well supported.
questions.hint: Consider how far the prediction extends beyond data.

questions.stem: If a forecast changes by 10 units when an assumption shifts by 2 percent, what is the sensitivity in units per percentage point?
questions.explanation: Divide the forecast change by the assumption shift: 10 divided by 2 equals 5 units per percentage point. This quantifies sensitivity.
questions.hint: Divide output change by input change.

questions.stem: A tree path has branches 0.4 and 0.25; what is the probability of following that path?
questions.explanation: Multiply along the path: 0.4 times 0.25 equals 0.10. This is the path probability.
questions.hint: Multiply the branch probabilities.

questions.stem: Given P(A)=0.4, P(B|A)=0.5 and P(B)=0.5, what is P(A|B)?
questions.explanation: Bayes gives 0.4 times 0.5 divided by 0.5, which equals 0.4. The reverse conditional is 0.4.
questions.hint: Apply Bayes theorem.

questions.stem: For 4 trials with success probability 0.5, what is the probability of exactly 2 successes?
questions.explanation: C(4,2) times 0.5 squared times 0.5 squared equals 6 times 0.0625, which is 0.375. The combination counts all orderings.
questions.hint: Include the combination and both outcomes.

questions.stem: A normal value at two standard deviations above the mean is approximately what percentile?

options.text: About the 99.85th percentile
About the 84th percentile
About the 97.5th percentile
About the 50th percentile

questions.explanation: About 97.5 percent fall below two standard deviations above the mean. That places it near the 97.5th percentile.
questions.hint: Add half the outside mass to 95 percent.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: Why is the normal distribution symmetric around its mean?

answer.exemplar: The density depends on squared distance from the mean, so values equally far above and below have equal probability.

questions.explanation: Probability depends on squared distance, making mirror values equally likely. Hence the distribution is symmetric.
questions.hint: Consider how distance enters the density.

questions.stem: A report says doubling sample size halves the standard error; is this correct?

options.text: Yes, but only for small samples
Yes, standard error is inversely proportional to n
No, doubling n has no effect on standard error
No, doubling n reduces standard error by a factor of root two, not two

questions.explanation: Standard error is sigma divided by root n, so doubling n divides by root 2, not 2. The report overstates the reduction.
questions.hint: Recall the square root in the denominator.

questions.stem: A convenience sample of shoppers at one store claims city-wide preferences; is the claim supported?

options.text: Yes, if the sample size is at least 30
No, one store's shoppers may not represent the whole city
Yes, because shoppers are a subset of city residents
No, surveys can never measure preferences

questions.explanation: Convenience sampling at one store may not mirror the city. The claim overreaches the sample's coverage.
questions.hint: Consider selection bias and coverage.

questions.stem: A regression assumes errors are independent; which situation most threatens this?

options.text: The sample size is larger than 30
The predictor has a wide range of values
options.misconception: confuses predictor spread with error dependence

options.text: Observations are collected in time order with autocorrelation
The outcome is measured in whole numbers

questions.explanation: Time-ordered data often exhibit autocorrelation, violating error independence. The other options do not threaten it.
questions.hint: Think about how errors might relate across observations.

questions.stem: A tree has two first-stage branches 0.7 and 0.3, with second-stage success probabilities 0.5 and 0.2; what is total success probability?
questions.explanation: Compute 0.7 times 0.5 plus 0.3 times 0.2, which is 0.35 plus 0.06 equals 0.41. This is the total success probability.
questions.hint: Sum the products of branch pairs.

questions.stem: Of 80 orders, 20 are express and 5 express ones are delayed; what is P(delayed | express)?
questions.explanation: Divide delayed express orders by all express orders: 5 divided by 20 equals 0.25. That is the conditional share.
questions.hint: Divide joint count by the condition count.
